assertion|assert: The macro `assert` from `<cassert>`, inherited from C; evaluates an expression and immediately terminates the program if it is false. For detecting programming errors. See [Errors, assertions and the trouble with error codes](#/comp3522-w5/errors-assertions).
NDEBUG: Defining `NDEBUG` before `#include <cassert>` turns every `assert` off. See [Errors, assertions and the trouble with error codes](#/comp3522-w5/errors-assertions).
error code: The C way: a function returns a number meaning success or failure (like `main` still does). Problems: it can be ignored, it uses up the return value, results must come back through pointer or reference arguments, and expressions cannot be built from the results. See [Errors, assertions and the trouble with error codes](#/comp3522-w5/errors-assertions).
exception: An object thrown with `throw` for a situation that prevents proper continuation of the program and cannot be handled locally. C++ lets you throw anything (strings, numbers, user types, standard-library exceptions); define a type or use a standard one. See [throw, try and catch](#/comp3522-w5/throw-try-catch).
throw: The statement that raises an exception: `throw cannot_open_file();`. A bare `throw;` inside a handler rethrows the current exception. See [throw, try and catch](#/comp3522-w5/throw-try-catch).
try-catch block|try|catch: `try { … } catch (type& e) { … }`: the try block holds code that may throw; the first catch block with a matching type runs. See [throw, try and catch](#/comp3522-w5/throw-try-catch).
catch by reference: Guideline 1: `catch (parent_type& e)` also captures exceptions derived from the reference type without slicing them. Catching by value copies and slices. See [The six catch guidelines and stack unwinding](#/comp3522-w5/catch-guidelines).
catch-all|ellipsis|catch (...): `catch (...)` catches every exception; it must be the last handler. See [The six catch guidelines and stack unwinding](#/comp3522-w5/catch-guidelines).
rethrow: Guideline 6: after an error message or a rescue, `throw;` sends the same exception on to an outer handler. See [The six catch guidelines and stack unwinding](#/comp3522-w5/catch-guidelines).
stack unwinding: While an exception travels up to a matching handler, every frame it leaves destroys its local objects in reverse order. See [The six catch guidelines and stack unwinding](#/comp3522-w5/catch-guidelines).
noexcept: A C++11 qualification promising that no exceptions must be thrown out of a function: `double square_root(double x) noexcept`. If one is thrown anyway, the program ends. Destructors are implicitly noexcept. See [noexcept, std::exception and terminate](#/comp3522-w5/noexcept-std-exceptions).
std: :exception: The base class in `<exception>` designed to be derived; every exception thrown by the standard library derives from it; has a virtual `what()` returning a null-terminated `const char*`. See [noexcept, std::exception and terminate](#/comp3522-w5/noexcept-std-exceptions).
what(): The virtual member function of `std::exception` that returns the message as a `const char*`; override it as `const char* what() const noexcept override`. See [noexcept, std::exception and terminate](#/comp3522-w5/noexcept-std-exceptions).
logic_error: In `<stdexcept>`, the family for errors in the program's logic: `invalid_argument`, `length_error`, `out_of_range`. See [noexcept, std::exception and terminate](#/comp3522-w5/noexcept-std-exceptions).
runtime_error: In `<stdexcept>`, the family for errors only detectable while running: `range_error`, `overflow_error`. See [noexcept, std::exception and terminate](#/comp3522-w5/noexcept-std-exceptions).
invalid_argument: A `logic_error` thrown when an argument is unacceptable, as in the `Name` constructor given an empty first name. See [noexcept, std::exception and terminate](#/comp3522-w5/noexcept-std-exceptions).
bad_alloc: Thrown by `new` on allocation failure. See [noexcept, std::exception and terminate](#/comp3522-w5/noexcept-std-exceptions).
terminate|std: :terminate: The function called when no catch statement matches a thrown exception (or a noexcept function throws); it calls the termination handler, which calls `abort`. See [noexcept, std::exception and terminate](#/comp3522-w5/noexcept-std-exceptions).
function-try-block: `C(int x) try : A(), my_b(x) { … } catch (...) { … }`: a try block wrapped around a constructor's initializer list and body; its handler always rethrows. See [noexcept, std::exception and terminate](#/comp3522-w5/noexcept-std-exceptions).
design principle: A high-level guideline for structuring components and managing their interactions (message passing, communication), as opposed to a design pattern, which tells how to design a system. See [Coupling, cohesion and dependencies](#/comp3522-w5/coupling-cohesion).
coupling: Links between separate units of a program; the strength of the connection between modules. Aim for loose coupling. See [Coupling, cohesion and dependencies](#/comp3522-w5/coupling-cohesion).
tight coupling|tightly coupled: Two classes depend closely on many details of each other; changes cascade, classes are harder to understand and test in isolation. A form of strong dependency. See [Coupling, cohesion and dependencies](#/comp3522-w5/coupling-cohesion).
loose coupling: The goal: understand one class without reading others, change one with little or no effect on others; increases maintainability. See [Coupling, cohesion and dependencies](#/comp3522-w5/coupling-cohesion).
cohesion: The number and diversity of tasks a single unit is responsible for; the glue that holds a module together. Aim for high cohesion: one single logical task per unit. See [Coupling, cohesion and dependencies](#/comp3522-w5/coupling-cohesion).
dependency: Entity A uses entity B, so A depends on B; a change in B may require a change in A. Entities always depend on each other in OOP; prefer weak dependencies through abstractions. See [Coupling, cohesion and dependencies](#/comp3522-w5/coupling-cohesion).
decoupling: Reducing dependencies between units, most commonly and effectively with inheritance and interfaces/abstract classes (Sushi → Filling; UI → DataSource). See [Coupling, cohesion and dependencies](#/comp3522-w5/coupling-cohesion).
SOLID: Five design principles for maintainable, decoupled, flexible object-oriented code, created by Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob"): Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion. See [Single Responsibility and Open/Closed](#/comp3522-w5/solid-srp-ocp).
Single Responsibility Principle|SRP: Each class is responsible for only one thing; there should be only one reason to change a class. See [Single Responsibility and Open/Closed](#/comp3522-w5/solid-srp-ocp).
Open/Closed Principle|OCP: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification: extend or inherit and override instead of editing the class for special cases. See [Single Responsibility and Open/Closed](#/comp3522-w5/solid-srp-ocp).
Liskov Substitution Principle|LSP: If S is a subtype of T, objects of type T may be replaced with objects of type S without altering the correctness of the program; refer to all child widgets as their base class. See [Liskov Substitution and Interface Segregation](#/comp3522-w5/solid-lsp-isp).
Interface Segregation Principle|ISP: Many client-specific interfaces are better than one general-purpose interface; no client should be forced to depend on functions it does not use. The SRP for interfaces. See [Liskov Substitution and Interface Segregation](#/comp3522-w5/solid-lsp-isp).
Dependency Inversion Principle|DIP: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions. See [Dependency Inversion and the Law of Demeter](#/comp3522-w5/dip-demeter).
high-level module: A module containing complex logic made of smaller chunks of simpler code (the UI class). See [Dependency Inversion and the Law of Demeter](#/comp3522-w5/dip-demeter).
low-level module: A class encapsulating simple atomic behaviour, such as reading and writing a file or displaying an image. See [Dependency Inversion and the Law of Demeter](#/comp3522-w5/dip-demeter).
Law of Demeter: Each unit should have only limited knowledge about other units, only those closely related; talk to your friends, not to strangers. Classes should know the public members of neighbouring classes, not of classes several hops away. See [Dependency Inversion and the Law of Demeter](#/comp3522-w5/dip-demeter).
train wreck: A chain such as `obj.getX().getY().getZ().doSomething()` that reaches through several classes; the Law of Demeter forbids it. See [Dependency Inversion and the Law of Demeter](#/comp3522-w5/dip-demeter).
